linkages: Adults are linked into households of one or two adults if they live together and either are married to each other or have entered into a registered partnership, or have at least one common child registered in the Civil Registration System, or are of opposite sex with an age difference of 15 years or less, are not closely related and live in a household with no other adults.

Children living with their parents are counted as members of the parents' family if they are under 25, have never married or entered a registered partnership and have no children of their own; where three or more generations share an address, the two younger generations form one family and the eldest generation a separate one.
Households are followed over the 13-year panel, with the head of household defined as the highest earner over the whole period; an individual's household changes on marriage or divorce.
Household-level balance sheets are linked to sector-level financial accounts from Danmarks Nationalbank so that aggregate URE and NNP exposure across the Danish economy sums to zero.
Household expenditure panels are linked to car registry data on the current value of cars owned, to build a nondurable consumption proxy.

sample.universe: Danish households of one or two adults whose head - the highest earner over the 13-year period - was aged between 30 and 55 in 2008
selection_rules: Define a household as one or two adults, using the marriage, common-child and age-difference criteria of section 4.1.
Define the head of household as the highest earner over the 13-year period in the sample.
Limit the sample to households headed by an individual between the ages of 30 and 55 in 2008, because the method requires income uncertainty to be relatively constant over the observed period.
Remove business owners, and all households receiving more than a trivial amount of their income from business ventures, because the expenditure imputation does not work for them.
Remove households in the top and bottom 1% of the income distribution.

Normalise income by average household income over the observed period and residualise it on dummies for age, year, highest level of education, marital status, homeowner status and number of children plus interactions of age with education, marital status and homeowner status.
Remove households in the top and bottom 1% of the unexpected income change distribution; apply the same steps to expenditure.

Exclude household-years in which the household is involved in a housing transaction (housing wealth is treated as off balance sheet for the imputation); this is the criterion that reduces the sample size the most.
Discard both income and expenditure data for household-years in which imputed expenditure is negative (about 3% of households).
Require households to survive as a household for at least five years, since growth over three, four and five years is used.
sample.period: 2004-2015 (register data 2003-2015; URE and NNP can only be calculated for 2009-2015 because mortgage information is insufficiently detailed in earlier years)
sample.n_observations: 7,664,360 household-year observations in the estimation sample (described in the text as 7.7 million), against 18,050,340 household-year observations in the age 30-55 population

construction_notes: Expenditure is imputed from the budget identity C-bar_t = Y-bar_t - S-bar_t = Y-bar_t - P_t - dNW_t, where P_t is contributions to privately administered pension schemes and dNW_t is the change in non-pension, non-housing net worth measured at the end of years t and t-1; banks and brokers must report client account values on 31 December and the tax year runs 1 January to 31 December, so income and wealth line up.

Expenditure includes durables (hence Marginal Propensity to eXpend) but excludes real estate; housing wealth is excluded from net worth for the imputation only, and the net wealth measure used where wealth itself is of interest (for example table II) includes housing.

Households holding equities are assumed to hold a diversified index of Danish stocks; only around 10% of Danish households hold any stocks. Pension flows are observed directly and treated as off balance sheet.
Income and expenditure are modelled in levels rather than logs, to allow direct estimates of marginal propensities; appendix J re-runs the analysis in logs, which yields elasticities.

Income is modelled in continuous time: a martingale permanent component plus a generically shaped transitory impulse f(t) that decays to zero within two years, time aggregated over each year (equation 1). The variance of N-year income growth is (N - 1/3) sigma_P^2 + 2 Var(y-tilde) for N >= 3, where the coefficient is N - 1/3 rather than N because of time aggregation.

Growth over three, four and five years is used, giving 96 moments (8 x (3 + 2 + 1) growth periods, each with a variance and a covariance moment) for four parameters. The Sargan-Hansen J-test null is strongly rejected, which the authors attribute to the sample size.
All values in table II are 2015 USD; age refers to age in 2008 of the main income earner. For the population consumption figures the top and bottom 1% of consumption are excluded.
Liquid wealth is defined as bank deposits, measured as mean household holdings over the entire sample period; net wealth is likewise a mean over the period.

URE is annual savings (after-tax income minus expenditure) plus maturing assets minus maturing liabilities: all bank deposits and bank debt are treated as floating rate, 20% of securities and of other liabilities is counted (a five-year maturity), and for mortgage debt the stock resetting over the coming 12 months is observed directly with the new rate applied for half the year. NNP is financial assets (deposits plus securities excluding shares) minus liabilities. Both are averages over 2009-2015 deflated by the CPI.

Bank deposits excluded from the microdata (children's savings accounts and some bank-administered pension savings, 33 billion USD) are grouped with pension fund assets; the maturity of non-household assets and liabilities is calibrated to 3.65 years so that total URE in the economy is zero.
The nondurable proxy subtracts the residualised change in car value scaled by 1/0.421, since car purchases make up 42.1% of durable expenditure in Denmark.
Estimation uses diagonally weighted minimum distance following Blundell, Pistaferri, and Preston (2008); the paper reports very similar results with optimal minimum distance.

claims.statement: A one-unit transitory increase in Danish household income raises imputed household expenditure in the same year by 0.50 units: the mean MPX out of transitory shocks in the estimation sample is 0.50.

treatment.label: transitory income shock (y-tilde, total transitory income received in the year)

register_source.value: Danish administrative tax records: after tax and transfer labour income of the head of household (the paper names no Statistics Denmark register or variable code)

definition.value: The transitory component of household labour income. Income is after tax and transfer labour income of the head of household (the highest earner over the 13-year period), normalised by average household income over the observed period and taken as the residual from a regression on dummies for age, year, highest level of education, marital status, homeowner status and number of children plus interactions of age with education, marital status and homeowner status. In continuous time the transitory impulse f(t) decays to zero within two years, and y-tilde_T is the time-aggregated transitory income received in year T (equation 4); its variance is identified from the variance of N-year income growth (equation 3). Modelled in levels, not logs.

timing.value: Received within the year in which the expenditure response is measured; the transitory income impulse has decayed to zero within two years

outcome.label: imputed household expenditure (c-tilde, the transitory consumption response)

register_source.value: Imputed from Danish administrative tax records on income and wealth; the paper names no Statistics Denmark register or variable code

definition.value: Expenditure imputed from the household budget identity C-bar_t = Y-bar_t - S-bar_t = Y-bar_t - P_t - dNW_t, where P_t is contributions to privately administered pension schemes and dNW_t is the change in non-pension, non-housing net worth measured at the end of years t and t-1. It includes durables (hence Marginal Propensity to eXpend rather than consume) but excludes real estate; housing wealth is left off balance sheet and years with a housing transaction are dropped. Expenditure is residualised and normalised exactly as income is. Total transitory consumption c-tilde_T is the time-aggregated response to transitory income impulses (equation 6).

timing.value: Annual, 2004-2015; the expenditure response measured in the same year as the income shock

units.value: units of expenditure per unit of transitory income (a marginal propensity to expend, dimensionless)

magnitude.interpretation: The paper calls this the average MPC in the economy, close to estimates obtained from natural experiments, and a little higher than most estimates in its table I, bearing in mind that it includes durables and is best compared to a six-month MPC.

estimand.time_horizon: the expenditure response within the same year as the transitory income shock; approximately a six-month MPX if transitory income shocks have no persistence

quintiles of net wealth averaged over the sample period

population.selection: Households of one or two adults whose head (the highest earner over the 13-year period) was aged 30 to 55 in 2008. Business owners and households receiving more than a trivial amount of income from business ventures are excluded; the top and bottom 1% of the income level distribution and of the unexpected income change distribution are removed; household-years with a housing transaction within the five-year window and household-years with negative imputed expenditure are dropped; households must survive as a household for at least five years.

identification.source_of_variation: No external shock or reform. Identification comes from covariance restrictions on panel data: the shape of the variance of N-year household income growth and of its covariance with N-year expenditure growth as the growth horizon N lengthens, because transitory shocks contribute a fixed amount of variance at the two ends of the window while permanent shocks accumulate linearly in N. Estimated on growth over three, four and five years in a continuous-time model that accounts for the time aggregation of annual data.

key_assumptions.assumption: Idiosyncratic income is the sum of a permanent component that follows a continuous-time martingale with independent increments (a random walk) and a transitory component that persists for no more than two years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix B (figure B.1) shows permanent and transitory shock variance are approximately constant and of similar size for heads aged 30 to 55; appendix H discusses the RIP versus HIP income process and shows the empirical variance of income growth is close to linear in N around N = 3, 4, 5; appendix B notes the variance of one-year growth is consistent with some persistence in the transitory component, which is why growth over one and two years is excluded.

formal.as_written: Var(Ps1 - Ps2 ) = (s1 - s2 )sigmaP2 ; Cov(Ps1 - Ps2 , Ps3 - Ps4 ) = 0 ; Ps = 0 if s < 0

key_assumptions.assumption: The consumption response to a transitory income shock follows a generic path g(t) that has fallen to zero two years after the news of the shock.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Gelman (2016) and Fagereng, Holm, and Natvik (2016) are cited as showing the response has entirely or almost entirely decayed two years after the shock; appendix F simulates the bias from slower decay (figure F.1) and table F.1 re-estimates psi with different pairs of growth horizons N.

formal.as_written: ct = phi Ps + integral_{t-2}^{t} g(t - s)dQs

key_assumptions.assumption: The consumption response to a permanent income shock follows a random walk proportional to the permanent shock.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix G writes down a model with durables and shows the durable component of the covariance cancels out, so the method identifies the non-durable permanent response phi_nd and psi but not phi_d.

key_assumptions.assumption: There is no measurement error in the observed changes in labour income.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 7.1.1 argues third-party reporting by employers, a high level of trust in institutions and a small black economy make underreporting very low, and that any growth in unreported income uncorrelated with reported income growth would not bias the estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Measurement error in imputed expenditure growth is uncorrelated with labour income growth.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Baker, Kueng, Pagel, and Meyer (2018) are cited as showing the relation between income and imputation error is economically small; appendix J re-estimates excluding households with more than USD 10,000 of stocks, keeping households with negative imputed expenditure, and with a 2.5% rather than 1% outlier cutoff.

key_assumptions.assumption: Idiosyncratic income risk (the variance of permanent and transitory shocks) is constant over the observed period.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The sample is limited to heads aged 30 to 55 in 2008 because appendix B (figure B.1) shows the variance is stable in that age range; appendix I simulates data with time-varying transitory risk matching the observed pattern and recovers phi and psi within 1% of their true values.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample conditions used to make the imputation work - surviving as a household for at least five years, making no housing transaction in the five-year window, reporting non-negative imputed expenditure, not being a business owner, and lying inside the top and bottom 1% cutoffs - are unrelated to the consumption response being estimated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix J re-estimates under alternative sample selection procedures and reports the results are qualitatively unchanged; the authors nevertheless concede that households changing through marriage and divorce leads to some selection bias.

key_assumptions.assumption: The expenditure response to positive and negative income shocks is symmetric, so that the estimate is an average of the two.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing: the authors state the assumption in a footnote and note that studies such as Bunn, Le Roux, Reinold, and Surico (2018) find a smaller MPC for positive than for negative shocks.

estimation.specification: Continuous-time model of permanent and transitory income and expenditure, time aggregated to annual frequency; moments are equations (3) and (5) evaluated at N = 3, 4, 5, giving 96 moments for four parameters (sigma_p^2, Var(y-tilde), phi, psi). The Sargan-Hansen J-test null is strongly rejected, which the authors attribute to the sample size.

ambiguities: Table F.1 in appendix F reports a pooled psi of 0.58 to 0.68 depending on which pair of growth horizons N is used, which is higher than the 0.50 quoted in section 5; the paper does not reconcile the two numbers, so they are recorded as separate claims rather than averaged.

definition.value: The transitory component of household labour income. Income is after tax and transfer labour income of the head of household (the highest earner over the 13-year period), normalised by average household income over the observed period and taken as the residual from a regression on dummies for age, year, highest level of education, marital status, homeowner status and number of children plus interactions of age with education, marital status and homeowner status. definition.value: The transitory component of household labour income. Income is after tax and transfer labour income of the head of household (the highest earner over the 13-year period), normalised by average household income over the observed period and taken as the residual from a regression on dummies for age, year, highest level of education, marital status, homeowner status and number of children plus interactions of age with education, marital status and homeowner status. In continuous time the transitory impulse f(t) decays to zero within two years, and y-tilde_T is the time-aggregated transitory income received in year T (equation 4); its variance is identified from the variance of N-year income growth (equation 3). Modelled in levels, not logs.

timing.value: Received within the year in which the expenditure response is measured; the transitory income impulse has decayed to zero within two years

outcome.label: imputed household expenditure (c-tilde, the transitory consumption response)

register_source.value: Imputed from Danish administrative tax records on income and wealth; the paper names no Statistics Denmark register or variable code

definition.value: Expenditure imputed from the household budget identity C-bar_t = Y-bar_t - S-bar_t = Y-bar_t - P_t - dNW_t, where P_t is contributions to privately administered pension schemes and dNW_t is the change in non-pension, non-housing net worth measured at the end of years t and t-1. It includes durables (hence Marginal Propensity to eXpend rather than consume) but excludes real estate; housing wealth is left off balance sheet and years with a housing transaction are dropped. Expenditure is residualised and normalised exactly as income is. Total transitory consumption c-tilde_T is the time-aggregated response to transitory income impulses (equation 6).

identification.source_of_variation: No external shock or reform. Identification comes from covariance restrictions on panel data: the shape of the variance of N-year household income growth and of its covariance with N-year expenditure growth as the growth horizon N lengthens, because transitory shocks contribute a fixed amount of variance at the two ends of the window while permanent shocks accumulate linearly in N. Estimated on growth over three, four and five years in a continuous-time model that accounts for the time aggregation of annual data.

definition.value: The transitory component of household labour income. Income is after tax and transfer labour income of the head of household (the highest earner over the 13-year period), normalised by average household income over the observed period and taken as the residual from a regression on dummies for age, year, highest level of education, marital status, homeowner status and number of children plus interactions of age with education, marital status and homeowner status. In continuous time the transitory impulse f(t) decays to zero within two years, and y-tilde_T is the time-aggregated transitory income received in year T (equation 4); its variance is identified from the variance of N-year income growth (equation 3). Modelled in levels, not logs.

definition.value: Expenditure imputed from the household budget identity C-bar_t = Y-bar_t - S-bar_t = Y-bar_t - P_t - dNW_t, where P_t is contributions to privately administered pension schemes and dNW_t is the change in non-pension, non-housing net worth measured at the end of years t and t-1. It includes durables (hence Marginal Propensity to eXpend rather than consume) but excludes real estate; housing wealth is left off balance sheet and years with a housing transaction are dropped. Expenditure is residualised and normalised exactly as income is. Total transitory consumption c-tilde_T is the time-aggregated response to transitory income impulses (equation 6).

estimation.specification: Continuous-time model of permanent and transitory income and expenditure, time aggregated to annual frequency; moments are equations (3) and (5) evaluated at N = 3, 4, 5, giving 96 moments for four parameters (sigma_p^2, Var(y-tilde), phi, psi). identification.source_of_variation: No external shock or reform. Identification comes from covariance restrictions on panel data: the shape of the variance of N-year household income growth and of its covariance with N-year expenditure growth as the growth horizon N lengthens, because transitory shocks contribute a fixed amount of variance at the two ends of the window while permanent shocks accumulate linearly in N. Estimated on growth over three, four and five years in a continuous-time model that accounts for the time aggregation of annual data.

key_assumptions.assumption: Idiosyncratic income is the sum of a permanent component that follows a continuous-time martingale with independent increments (a random walk) and a transitory component that persists for no more than two years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix B (figure B.1) shows permanent and transitory shock variance are approximately constant and of similar size for heads aged 30 to 55; appendix H discusses the RIP versus HIP income process and shows the empirical variance of income growth is close to linear in N around N = 3, 4, 5; appendix B notes the variance of one-year growth is consistent with some persistence in the transitory component, which is why growth over one and two years is excluded.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing: the authors state the assumption in a footnote and note that studies such as Bunn, Le Roux, Reinold, and Surico (2018) find a smaller MPC for positive than for negative shocks.

identification.source_of_variation: No external shock or reform. Identification comes from covariance restrictions on panel data: the shape of the variance of N-year household income growth and of its covariance with N-year expenditure growth as the growth horizon N lengthens, because transitory shocks contribute a fixed amount of variance at the two ends of the window while permanent shocks accumulate linearly in N. Estimated on growth over three, four and five years in a continuous-time model that accounts for the time aggregation of annual data.

key_assumptions.assumption: Idiosyncratic income is the sum of a permanent component that follows a continuous-time martingale with independent increments (a random walk) and a transitory component that persists for no more than two years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix B (figure B.1) shows permanent and transitory shock variance are approximately constant and of similar size for heads aged 30 to 55; appendix H discusses the RIP versus HIP income process and shows the empirical variance of income growth is close to linear in N around N = 3, 4, 5; appendix B notes the variance of one-year growth is consistent with some persistence in the transitory component, which is why growth over one and two years is excluded.

formal.as_written: Var(Ps1 - Ps2 ) = (s1 - s2 )sigmaP2 ; Cov(Ps1 - Ps2 , Ps3 - Ps4 ) = 0 ; Ps = 0 if s < 0

key_assumptions.assumption: The consumption response to a transitory income shock follows a generic path g(t) that has fallen to zero two years after the news of the shock.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Gelman (2016) and Fagereng, Holm, and Natvik (2016) are cited as showing the response has entirely or almost entirely decayed two years after the shock; appendix F simulates the bias from slower decay (figure F.1) and table F.1 re-estimates psi with different pairs of growth horizons N.

formal.as_written: ct = phi Ps + integral_{t-2}^{t} g(t - s)dQs

key_assumptions.assumption: The consumption response to a permanent income shock follows a random walk proportional to the permanent shock.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix G writes down a model with durables and shows the durable component of the covariance cancels out, so the method identifies the non-durable permanent response phi_nd and psi but not phi_d.

key_assumptions.assumption: There is no measurement error in the observed changes in labour income.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 7.1.1 argues third-party reporting by employers, a high level of trust in institutions and a small black economy make underreporting very low, and that any growth in unreported income uncorrelated with reported income growth would not bias the estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Measurement error in imputed expenditure growth is uncorrelated with labour income growth.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Baker, Kueng, Pagel, and Meyer (2018) are cited as showing the relation between income and imputation error is economically small; appendix J re-estimates excluding households with more than USD 10,000 of stocks, keeping households with negative imputed expenditure, and with a 2.5% rather than 1% outlier cutoff.

key_assumptions.assumption: Idiosyncratic income risk (the variance of permanent and transitory shocks) is constant over the observed period.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The sample is limited to heads aged 30 to 55 in 2008 because appendix B (figure B.1) shows the variance is stable in that age range; appendix I simulates data with time-varying transitory risk matching the observed pattern and recovers phi and psi within 1% of their true values.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample conditions used to make the imputation work - surviving as a household for at least five years, making no housing transaction in the five-year window, reporting non-negative imputed expenditure, not being a business owner, and lying inside the top and bottom 1% cutoffs - are unrelated to the consumption response being estimated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix J re-estimates under alternative sample selection procedures and reports the results are qualitatively unchanged; the authors nevertheless concede that households changing through marriage and divorce leads to some selection bias.

key_assumptions.assumption: The expenditure response to positive and negative income shocks is symmetric, so that the estimate is an average of the two.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing: the authors state the assumption in a footnote and note that studies such as Bunn, Le Roux, Reinold, and Surico (2018) find a smaller MPC for positive than for negative shocks.

threats_discussed: time aggregation of annual income and expenditure data (Working 1960), which biases the BPP covariance-restriction method
measurement error in imputed expenditure from capital gains on directly held stocks
transfers of wealth between family members or friends, which would bias the MPX up if family actively insures labour income
off-balance-sheet saving, which the imputation would read as expenditure and which would raise the estimated MPX one for one
durable goods: a delay between a permanent income shock and the durable purchase biases the transitory MPX up
persistence of the consumption response beyond two years, which biases the transitory MPX down
misspecification of the income process (RIP versus HIP; an AR(1) rather than random walk permanent component)
time-varying idiosyncratic income risk over the great recession
sample selection from the five-year survival, housing-transaction and non-negative-expenditure requirements
running the regressions in levels rather than logs over long growth horizons
robustness_checks: re-estimating psi using every pair of growth horizons N = n1, n2 from 1 to 6 (table F.1)
simulating data with exponentially decaying and Fagereng-Holm-Natvik consumption responses to gauge the bias from persistence (figures F.1 and F.2)
excluding households holding more than USD 10,000 of stocks (figure J.2)
keeping households with negative imputed expenditure (figure J.2)
a stricter 2.5% rather than 1% outlier cutoff on the level and change of income and expenditure (figure J.2)
specifying income and expenditure in logs rather than levels, yielding elasticities (figure J.3)
using total household income rather than the household head's income (figure J.4)
quintiles of liquid wealth divided by permanent income rather than absolute liquid wealth (figure J.5)
a nondurable expenditure proxy built from car registry data, and an expenditure panel excluding cars (figure IX)
applying BPP's original method to the Danish moments (appendix E)
optimal rather than diagonally weighted minimum distance
simulating time-varying income risk (appendix I)
unresolved_confounders: off-balance-sheet saving (offshore or non-financial assets), which would raise the estimated MPX one for one for every percentage point of income shocks saved that way
active insurance of labour income between friends and family, which would bias the MPX estimates upward
mis-measured idiosyncratic stock returns, which the authors say could bias the MPX by no more than a few percentage points
a consumption response to transitory shocks that decays more slowly than two years, which the authors say likely leaves a slight downward bias across the range of MPCs
a delay between a permanent income shock and the purchase of durables, which biases the transitory MPX upward
whether income follows a Restricted or a Heterogeneous Income Profile, which appendix H says the data cannot distinguish
selection bias from households changing composition through marriage and divorce, given the five-year survival requirement

population.selection: Households of one or two adults whose head (the highest earner over the 13-year period) was aged 30 to 55 in 2008. Business owners and households receiving more than a trivial amount of income from business ventures are excluded; the top and bottom 1% of the income level distribution and of the unexpected income change distribution are removed; household-years with a housing transaction within the five-year window and household-years with negative imputed expenditure are dropped; households must survive as a household for at least five years.

identification.source_of_variation: No external shock or reform. Identification comes from covariance restrictions on panel data: the shape of the variance of N-year household income growth and of its covariance with N-year expenditure growth as the growth horizon N lengthens, because transitory shocks contribute a fixed amount of variance at the two ends of the window while permanent shocks accumulate linearly in N. Estimated on growth over three, four and five years in a continuous-time model that accounts for the time aggregation of annual data.

key_assumptions.assumption: Idiosyncratic income is the sum of a permanent component that follows a continuous-time martingale with independent increments (a random walk) and a transitory component that persists for no more than two years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix B (figure B.1) shows permanent and transitory shock variance are approximately constant and of similar size for heads aged 30 to 55; appendix H discusses the RIP versus HIP income process and shows the empirical variance of income growth is close to linear in N around N = 3, 4, 5; appendix B notes the variance of one-year growth is consistent with some persistence in the transitory component, which is why growth over one and two years is excluded.

formal.as_written: Var(Ps1 - Ps2 ) = (s1 - s2 )sigmaP2 ; Cov(Ps1 - Ps2 , Ps3 - Ps4 ) = 0 ; Ps = 0 if s < 0

key_assumptions.assumption: The consumption response to a transitory income shock follows a generic path g(t) that has fallen to zero two years after the news of the shock.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Gelman (2016) and Fagereng, Holm, and Natvik (2016) are cited as showing the response has entirely or almost entirely decayed two years after the shock; appendix F simulates the bias from slower decay (figure F.1) and table F.1 re-estimates psi with different pairs of growth horizons N.

formal.as_written: ct = phi Ps + integral_{t-2}^{t} g(t - s)dQs

key_assumptions.assumption: The consumption response to a permanent income shock follows a random walk proportional to the permanent shock.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix G writes down a model with durables and shows the durable component of the covariance cancels out, so the method identifies the non-durable permanent response phi_nd and psi but not phi_d.

key_assumptions.assumption: There is no measurement error in the observed changes in labour income.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 7.1.1 argues third-party reporting by employers, a high level of trust in institutions and a small black economy make underreporting very low, and that any growth in unreported income uncorrelated with reported income growth would not bias the estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Measurement error in imputed expenditure growth is uncorrelated with labour income growth.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Baker, Kueng, Pagel, and Meyer (2018) are cited as showing the relation between income and imputation error is economically small; appendix J re-estimates excluding households with more than USD 10,000 of stocks, keeping households with negative imputed expenditure, and with a 2.5% rather than 1% outlier cutoff.

key_assumptions.assumption: Idiosyncratic income risk (the variance of permanent and transitory shocks) is constant over the observed period.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The sample is limited to heads aged 30 to 55 in 2008 because appendix B (figure B.1) shows the variance is stable in that age range; appendix I simulates data with time-varying transitory risk matching the observed pattern and recovers phi and psi within 1% of their true values.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample conditions used to make the imputation work - surviving as a household for at least five years, making no housing transaction in the five-year window, reporting non-negative imputed expenditure, not being a business owner, and lying inside the top and bottom 1% cutoffs - are unrelated to the consumption response being estimated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix J re-estimates under alternative sample selection procedures and reports the results are qualitatively unchanged; the authors nevertheless concede that households changing through marriage and divorce leads to some selection bias.

key_assumptions.assumption: The expenditure response to positive and negative income shocks is symmetric, so that the estimate is an average of the two.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing: the authors state the assumption in a footnote and note that studies such as Bunn, Le Roux, Reinold, and Surico (2018) find a smaller MPC for positive than for negative shocks.

claims.statement: For the wealthy hand-to-mouth: the first five URE deciles, with high homeownership rates but few liquid assets, the MPX out of transitory income is around 0.5.

treatment.label: transitory income shock (y-tilde, total transitory income received in the year)

register_source.value: Danish administrative tax records: after tax and transfer labour income of the head of household (the paper names no Statistics Denmark register or variable code)

definition.value: The transitory component of household labour income. Income is after tax and transfer labour income of the head of household (the highest earner over the 13-year period), normalised by average household income over the observed period and taken as the residual from a regression on dummies for age, year, highest level of education, marital status, homeowner status and number of children plus interactions of age with education, marital status and homeowner status. In continuous time the transitory impulse f(t) decays to zero within two years, and y-tilde_T is the time-aggregated transitory income received in year T (equation 4); its variance is identified from the variance of N-year income growth (equation 3). Modelled in levels, not logs.

timing.value: Received within the year in which the expenditure response is measured; the transitory income impulse has decayed to zero within two years

outcome.label: imputed household expenditure (c-tilde, the transitory consumption response)

register_source.value: Imputed from Danish administrative tax records on income and wealth; the paper names no Statistics Denmark register or variable code

definition.value: Expenditure imputed from the household budget identity C-bar_t = Y-bar_t - S-bar_t = Y-bar_t - P_t - dNW_t, where P_t is contributions to privately administered pension schemes and dNW_t is the change in non-pension, non-housing net worth measured at the end of years t and t-1. It includes durables (hence Marginal Propensity to eXpend rather than consume) but excludes real estate; housing wealth is left off balance sheet and years with a housing transaction are dropped. Expenditure is residualised and normalised exactly as income is. Total transitory consumption c-tilde_T is the time-aggregated response to transitory income impulses (equation 6).

timing.value: Annual, 2004-2015; the expenditure response measured in the same year as the income shock

units.value: units of expenditure per unit of transitory income (a marginal propensity to expend, dimensionless)

magnitude.interpretation: These households have relatively high MPXs, and it is likely that their wealth is locked up in illiquid assets (mostly housing) and that they have large mortgages.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample conditions used to make the imputation work - surviving as a household for at least five years, making no housing transaction in the five-year window, reporting non-negative imputed expenditure, not being a business owner, and lying inside the top and bottom 1% cutoffs - are unrelated to the consumption response being estimated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix J re-estimates under alternative sample selection procedures and reports the results are qualitatively unchanged; the authors nevertheless concede that households changing through marriage and divorce leads to some selection bias.

key_assumptions.assumption: The expenditure response to positive and negative income shocks is symmetric, so that the estimate is an average of the two.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Nothing: the authors state the assumption in a footnote and note that studies such as Bunn, Le Roux, Reinold, and Surico (2018) find a smaller MPC for positive than for negative shocks.

claims.statement: Permanent income uncertainty is highest for households in the lowest quintile of liquid wealth, and is remarkably similar across the top three quintiles at just over 0.002 per year.

treatment.label: quintile of liquid wealth, defined as bank deposits averaged over the sample period

register_source.value: Danish administrative tax records on wealth: bank deposits (the paper names no Statistics Denmark register or variable code)

definition.value: Liquid wealth is defined as bank deposits; households are divided into quintiles by mean household wealth holdings over the entire sample period. The paper notes the results are little changed under any other definition of liquid wealth as long as housing and debts are excluded. The lowest quintile holds less than $2,000 in bank deposits on average and the top quintile more than $30,000 (2015 USD).

timing.value: Mean holdings over the whole 2004-2015 observation window, i.e. not pre-determined relative to the income shocks

outcome.label: sigma_p^2, the variance of permanent income shocks

definition.value: The annual variance of permanent income shocks, Var(P_s1 - P_s2) = (s1 - s2) sigma_P^2, estimated for each group by GMM from the rate at which the variance of N-year income growth rises with N (equation 3).

timing.value: Per year, over the 2004-2015 estimation window

units.value: variance of permanent income shocks per year, in units of squared normalised income; the quoted figure is 'just over 0.002' for the top three quintiles, a standard deviation of just below 5% of permanent income per year

magnitude.interpretation: The paper reads the high permanent income uncertainty of the least liquid households, despite their low buffer stock, as evidence that heterogeneous tastes may matter more than income risk in determining wealth held for precautionary saving; and notes permanent income variance in Denmark is slightly higher than transitory variance, likely because of high social insurance.

population.selection: Households of one or two adults whose head (the highest earner over the 13-year period) was aged 30 to 55 in 2008. Business owners and households receiving more than a trivial amount of income from business ventures are excluded; the top and bottom 1% of the income level distribution and of the unexpected income change distribution are removed; household-years with a housing transaction within the five-year window and household-years with negative imputed expenditure are dropped; households must survive as a household for at least five years.

identification.source_of_variation: No external shock or reform. Identification comes from covariance restrictions on panel data: the shape of the variance of N-year household income growth and of its covariance with N-year expenditure growth as the growth horizon N lengthens, because transitory shocks contribute a fixed amount of variance at the two ends of the window while permanent shocks accumulate linearly in N. Estimated on growth over three, four and five years in a continuous-time model that accounts for the time aggregation of annual data.

key_assumptions.assumption: Idiosyncratic income is the sum of a permanent component that follows a continuous-time martingale with independent increments (a random walk) and a transitory component that persists for no more than two years.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix B (figure B.1) shows permanent and transitory shock variance are approximately constant and of similar size for heads aged 30 to 55; appendix H discusses the RIP versus HIP income process and shows the empirical variance of income growth is close to linear in N around N = 3, 4, 5; appendix B notes the variance of one-year growth is consistent with some persistence in the transitory component, which is why growth over one and two years is excluded.
